The VCF 9.1 VPC Networking Mental Model
1VCF 9.1 VPC Networking, Part 1: From External Connection to VPCYou are here

4VCF 9.1 VPC Networking, Part 4: VLAN Extension Under the HoodComing soon
5VCF 9.1 VPC Networking, Part 5: Four Gates for VPC TrafficComing soon
6VCF 9.1 VPC Networking, Part 6: The VPC North-South Firewall and Its CoverageComing soon

This is Part 1 of the series The VCF 9.1 VPC Networking Mental Model. It covers the order in which a Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) is built, from the provider’s External Connection down to the workload subnets. Later parts go deeper into each object.

VPC networking in VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9.1 is easiest to understand as a controlled hand-off. The default project holds the provider-owned constructs: External IP blocks and External Connections. A project is granted access to the ones it needs. Inside that project, a Transit Gateway sets the northbound model, a VPC consumes the matching connectivity and service profiles, and subnets become the networks the workloads sit on.

Core idea

Build the provider-side connectivity first. Delegate it to the project. Then let the project consume the correct transit, connectivity, and service profiles.

In everyday terms, think of a large apartment building. The provider is the building manager. They own the street entrance (the External Connection) and decide which flat numbers exist (the IP blocks). Each project is a tenant who rents a floor and arranges the flats on it (the VPCs) as they like. Tenants never build a new door to the street. They use the entrance the manager gave them.

1. Start in the default project

The default project is where the provider builds reusable external connectivity. Create the External IP Blocks needed for public subnets, External IPs, and NAT-translated addresses. Then define the External Connection that describes how the VPC domain reaches the physical network.

Choose the External Connection type

The External Connection is not just a label. Its type decides the data path and which centralized services are possible.

  • A Centralized Connection links the Transit Gateway through a Tier-0 gateway on NSX Edge nodes. The design guide lists stateful services for this model: Default Outbound NAT, custom NAT, Gateway Firewall, External IPs, load balancing, and VPN.
  • A Distributed VLAN Connection gives lightweight connectivity to the data centre fabric with no NSX Edge nodes and no dynamic routing. Stateful services run on Virtual Network Appliances (VNAs). The design guide also describes a VLAN Backed VPC model, introduced in 9.1.1, for TEP-less designs. Part 4 covers it.
  • A Distributed VXLAN Connection integrates with a standards-based EVPN-VXLAN fabric. The design guide lists it for 9.1.1. It needs EVPN Route Controller nodes to exchange BGP EVPN routes, and VNAs for stateful services.

2. Delegate provider constructs to the project

Projects give administrative and configuration isolation. Before a project administrator can build a VPC, the provider must grant the project access to the right External Connection and External IP Blocks. This delegation is the control point. It stops a project from consuming arbitrary provider networks or address space.

Note

Architecture check. A Transit Gateway can have several External Connections, but they must all be the same type: all centralized or all distributed. A VPC connects to only one Transit Gateway.

3. Create the project Transit Gateway

Move into the target project. Create the Transit Gateway from Networking, VPC Connectivity, Transit Gateways. Select the External Connection shared in the previous step. The Transit Gateway provides both inter-VPC communication and the connection to the outside network.

  • Select the delegated External Connection.
  • Enter the VPC External IP Blocks the gateway design needs.
  • Add Private Transit Gateway IP Blocks when private transit addressing is part of the model.
  • Confirm the connection type and the network span before attaching VPCs.
Tip

The project now has a defined path to the external network and the addressing it needs for VPC connectivity. Check that everything shows as realized before you go on.

4. Create the VPC with the matching profiles

In the target project, open the VPCs tab and click Add VPC. Enter the private VPC CIDRs, select the VPC Connectivity Profile, and check the External and Private TGW IP blocks it brings. The profile is the reusable northbound configuration the VPC consumes.

Service profile and Avi integration

A VPC Service Profile holds the DHCP server or relay settings and the subnet profiles. Avi is a separate setting on the VPC. Turn on Enable for Avi Load Balancer so the Avi Load Balancer Controller can discover the VPC. The toggle has two conditions: at least one private IP block and at least one edge cluster assigned to the VPC. The private block is needed because the virtual service IP sits on a private subnet. The edge cluster lets the Service Engines get addresses from the DHCP server.

5. Create workload-facing VPC subnets

Create subnets only after the VPC has the right northbound and service context. Choose the access mode and the address source on purpose. Public subnets take addresses from an External IP block. Private-TGW subnets take them from the Private TGW IP block. Private-VPC subnets take them from the VPC’s private CIDR. VLAN extension uses a Distributed VLAN Connection and is covered in Part 4.

Validation checklist

  • All External Connections and External IP Blocks show successful realization.
  • The project sees only the provider constructs meant for it.
  • The Transit Gateway uses the correct connection type and External Connection.
  • The VPC consumes the intended connectivity and service profiles.
  • External IP blocks do not overlap within the project or on the same Tier-0 gateway. Subnets match their Public, Private or VLAN intent.
  • Routes are present in NSX and in the physical network where advertisement is needed.
  • NAT, firewall and external reachability behave as designed.
  • VPCs with Enable for Avi Load Balancer on have a private IP block and an edge cluster assigned.

Design takeaways

Takeaway Why
Provider first External Connections and External IP Blocks start in the default project and are shared with projects.
Match the model Centralized, Distributed VLAN and Distributed VXLAN are different data-plane designs. All connections on one Transit Gateway must be the same type.
Edges only where required A centralized connection uses a Tier-0 gateway on NSX Edge nodes. A Distributed VLAN connection needs no Edge nodes. Its stateful services run on VNAs.
Profiles carry intent Connectivity and service profiles let many VPCs consume the same northbound and service configuration.

Official references

  • External Connections
  • Transit Gateways
  • Add a VPC Connectivity Profile
  • Add a VPC Service Profile
  • Configure VLAN-backed VPC Subnets in VCF 9.1
  • Add an External Connection for Distributed VXLAN Connectivity

What’s next

Part 2 takes each object from this build order and explains what it does: the IP blocks and why there are several, what an External Connection defines, how the Transit Gateway and the Connectivity Profile fit, the three subnet access modes, and where NAT comes in.

About the co-author

This series is co-written with Abhilash Pillai, an Architect in Broadcom’s VCF Division. Over the past 16 years he has designed and delivered network, security, data centre, and cloud platforms. He holds the CCDE, CCIE Routing and Switching, CCIE Security, CISSP, CCSK, TOGAF and multiple VCF VCAP certifications.

item.content:encoded:
We’re excited to announce the first VMmark benchmark results using new AMD EPYC 9006 Series Server CPUs. Submitted by Dell Technologies across 1-socket PowerEdge R9815 and 2-socket PowerEdge R9825 configurations, these two server platforms set a number of records in both performance and power-performance: see the VMmark Results page for more information.

Here are some of the highlights:

  • The PowerEdge R9815 and R9825 lead the VMmark 1-socket and 2-socket server performance categories, respectively.
  • They also have the top-ranked VMmark Performance-Per-Kilowatt (PPKW) scores in both Server Power-Performance and Server and Storage Power-Performance categories, which were added in VMmark 4.1. For more information, see: Introducing VMmark 4.1: Enhanced Power Efficiency Benchmarking for Private Cloud Infrastructure
  • These systems are powered by new 6th Generation AMD EPYC 9996 “Venice” CPUs featuring 256 cores, 512 threads, and 1024 MB L3 cache.
  • By enabling the latest CPU architectures, Broadcom, through VMware Cloud Foundation, brings each new CPU generation to private cloud infrastructure with scale and efficiency you can measure.

Let’s compare a 5th Generation AMD EPYC “Turin” VMmark result to one on the new 6th Generation AMD EPYC “Venice” platform to see how performance scales across generations:

VCF 9.1.2 enables support for these new CPUs, but performance across 9.1 maintenance releases remains virtually unchanged. The significant score jump is driven entirely by the new hardware generation.

A 60% increase in core count translates directly into a 70% higher VMmark score. By sustaining 5.8 tiles (121 VMs) compared to the R7715’s 3.8 tiles (77 VMs)—where each tile simulates a realistic mix of modern data center workloads—the R9815 drives a 57% increase in workload capacity. For private cloud environments, this means organizations can handle significantly higher compute demand while consolidating onto fewer physical servers during a hardware refresh.

Here are some resources to learn more:

  • VMmark 4
  • VMmark Community
  • VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1
  • Dell PowerEdge R9815, R9825
  • AMD EPYC 9006 Server CPUs

These comparisons are based on all VMmark results published as of 11/10/2026. VMmark is a free benchmarking tool provided as-is by Broadcom and used by partners and customers to measure the performance, scalability, and power consumption of virtualization platforms.

item.content:encoded:
In VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) Operations 9.1 the Broadcom team has re-engineered the Diagnostics Management Pack. We split the Diagnostics Management Pack into two parts, the Diagnostics Management Pack and the Diagnostics Content Pack, so we can deliver findings more quickly to our customers. 

When the findings were bundled into the Diagnostics Management pack, they were released along with product releases. This limited the number of finding releases and increased the time to inform customers of new security vulnerabilities and known issues in their environments. Splitting the findings out of this management pack allows us to add content packs to the Solution Catalog and not tie finding releases to solely product releases. The best way to think of this is the Anti-Virus definition model: the Diagnostics Management Pack is the required engine component and the Diagnostics Content Pack is the definition file that gives signatures of the known vulnerabilities. A new feature alerts customers when a new content pack is released to the solution catalog. From the Active Findings screen and Findings Catalog, customers will see the following notification banner. 

In the first content pack that we released to both VCF Operations 9.1.0 and 9.1.1, we included security-based, adoption blocking, and high global support trending issues. Most of the proceeding content packs will be focused on VMSA/CVE type findings. Below are some highlights of the findings in this content pack. 

Security Vulnerabilities

In VMSA-2026-0006, Broadcom informs customers of multiple CVEs impacting both vCenter and ESX. VMware vCenter contains an authentication bypass vulnerability in the VMware Directory Service (CVE-2026-59309). A malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this issue to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system. VMware vCenter contains a directory traversal vulnerability in the Syslog server (CVE-2026-59310). A malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this issue to execute arbitrary code. VMware ESX contains an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the VMXNET3 virtual network adapter. A malicious actor with local administrative privileges on a virtual machine with VMXNET3 virtual network adapter may exploit this issue to execute code on the host. 

vCenter_CVE_2026_59309to10_VMSA_202606 / ESX_CVE_2026_47876_VMSA_202606

  • https://support.broadcom.com/web/ecx/support-content-notification/-/external/content/SecurityAdvisories/0/38017
  • Critical

VCF Adoption Blocking Issues

Broadcom Technical Support has been focusing on resolving adoption blocking issues. One of the findings found in the content pack is a vCenter UUID case mismatch which impacts vCenter licensing. This is a vCenter Instance UUID case mismatch between vCenter and VCF Operations that causes this issue. This issue is resolved in VMware vCenter 9.1.0.0200. The workaround for this issue is to match the UUID case between VCF Operations and vCenter server. 

vCenter_UUIDCaseMismatch_KB_440982

  • https://knowledge.broadcom.com/external/article/440982
  • Immediate

Broadcom Technical Support Trending Issues

Broadcom Technical Support trending issues are Knowledge Base articles that have solved many cases and/or are viewed many times. One of the findings in the content pack is a vCenter login failure. This can happen when the client credentials used by the vCenter’s oauth2 client becomes invalid because it has expired. In VCF 9.0, there is a logic to rotate the vCenter’s OAuth2 client credentials every 90 days. This issue is resolved in vCenter 9.0.2 and workarounds are available in 9.0.0 and 9.0.1. 

vCenter_oauth2credentialsinvalid_KB_414489

  • https://knowledge.broadcom.com/external/article/414489
  • Immediate

We plan on releasing more Diagnostics Content Packs in the next coming weeks. Please subscribe to KB https://knowledge.broadcom.com/external/article/371661 for the latest updates.

item.content:encoded:
For modern enterprise development teams, release velocity relies heavily on instant access to realistic, production-mirrored environments. Every new feature, platform upgrade, or bug fix requires a secure, isolated space for testing. However, when platform engineers must manually provision, populate, and tear down these ephemeral environments using separate command-line tools, the result is an operational bottleneck. Manual cluster management can slow down developer access, introduce configuration drift, and lead to costly infrastructure sprawl across the data center.

To quantify the business value of transitioning to a declarative, GitOps-driven private cloud model, Broadcom commissioned Principled Technologies (PT) to conduct a hands-on testing validation study. The newly released report details how VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) Automation, leveraging its VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) Cluster Management capability, Argo CD, and Velero, transforms complex environment lifecycles into a governed, public cloud-like service.

Here’s why IT executives and cloud architects should examine the findings.

Slash Operational Toil to Reclaim Platform Engineering Bandwidth

Platform engineering talent is a premium resource that should be focused on strategic architecture, not repetitive ticketing requests. The PT study revealed that using VCF Automation reduces the hands-on administrative time required to create, manage, and delete a full-stack ephemeral development environment by up to 79.8 percent compared to manual execution.

By unifying infrastructure as code, VCF Automation compressed the end-to-end lifecycle from a manual 21 minutes and 20 seconds down to 4 minutes and 18 seconds per environment. For an enterprise processing 1,000 ephemeral environment requests annually, this efficiency could return an estimated 284 hours to the platform team. This can help platform teams scale their Kubernetes footprint without scaling headcount at the same rate.

Accelerate Developer Velocity While Preventing Configuration Drift

Providing developers with empty Kubernetes clusters is insufficient; they need accurate production data to validate their code reliably. The traditional manual approach requires administrators to download clients, manage object storage credentials, and install Velero servers across multiple clusters—a multi-step process that can introduce errors.

VCF Automation natively provides data protection built into its VKS Cluster Management capability. PT found that the guided, repeatable workflow takes 80.6 percent less hands-on time to securely back up a production environment and restore it into a development environment. By replacing disparate CLI tasks with a unified platform experience, IT can get production-mirrored data to developers faster while minimizing the risk of configuration drift.

Reclaim Hardware CapEx Through Automated Sprawl Prevention

One of the hidden financial drains of manual infrastructure management is “zombie” environments. These are clusters that are forgotten after testing concludes, and silently consume compute, storage, power, and licensing capacity.

Because VCF Automation can define each environment in Git, administrators can tear down entire infrastructure stacks with a single commit. The PT report highlights that cleanly deleting an environment takes merely 7 seconds of administrative time with VCF Automation, compared to 55 seconds of manual CLI deletion. For a large organization, curtailing this infrastructure sprawl could avoid roughly 115 orphaned environments at any given time, potentially avoiding up to $345,000 in annual operating and hardware capacity costs. (See report for assumptions; actual savings vary by environment.)

Transform your private cloud operations. Download and read the full Principled Technologies report to explore the complete testing methodology and discover how VCF Automation can help developers get production-mirrored ephemeral environments faster on the private cloud infrastructure you already own.

item.content:encoded:
Enabling the vSphere Supervisor in VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) involves choosing a network stack for workloads running on vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS), KubeVM Service, or Container Service – VCF Networking with Virtual Private Cloud (VPC), or the vSphere Distributed Switch. VCF Networking with VPC is the recommended, default option. It keeps Kubernetes nodes off the routable network, scales load balancing across up to ten appliance nodes instead of one active/standby pair, and opens up self-service networking, multi-tenancy, and third-party fabric integration that the vSphere Distributed Switch path can’t match [1][2].

For network decision makers planning VCF 9.1 deployments, VPC-based networking is the architecture built to scale with Kubernetes adoption.

Network stack choices

VCF 9.1 supports two different network stacks for the vSphere Supervisor. One is the vSphere Distributed Switch with a Foundation Load Balancer appliance. The other is VCF Networking with VPC, built on VMware VPCs behind a Transit Gateway[3]. Both stacks run virtual machines and VKS clusters side by side; the differences show up in exposure, scale, and how much room each one leaves to grow.

The vSphere Distributed Switch model connects Kubernetes cluster nodes directly to an existing VLAN, and a single Foundation Load Balancer appliance pair, running active/standby, handles every virtual IP address (VIP) in the environment [1][4]. VCF Networking with VPC takes a different approach: it places VKS cluster nodes on private networks with no direct external access, and distributes load-balancing and network address translation (NAT) services across a cluster of up to ten Virtual Network Appliance nodes running active/active [1][2]. A Transit Gateway connects those VPCs, either through a VLAN in a Distributed connection or through an NSX Edge cluster in a Centralized connection [3].

Let’s take a closer look at these options and see why VPC is the recommended network stack for VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF), and the required network stack for VCF Automation environments.

Important Considerations for Network Decision Makers

1. Private networks limit exposure and preserve IP space

With VPC-based networking, Kubernetes cluster nodes have no direct external access. They sit on private subnets and expose only the application endpoints that need to be reachable, through the load balancer. That matters for two practical reasons. It shrinks the attack surface, because nodes running workloads are frequent exploit targets, and keeping them off directly routable networks limits what an attacker can reach [9]. It also removes a scaling constraint: clusters on the vSphere Distributed Switch path are limited by how the physical VLAN was pre-provisioned, while VPC subnets auto-scale and use outbound NAT to reach outside resources without consuming routable address space for every node.

This follows best practices for running a Kubernetes service on any cloud – start with private nodes and add public exposure “only when the workload requires it,” paired with NAT for outbound access. The Kubernetes project’s own security checklist calls for the Kubernetes API server, kubelet API, and etcd to stay unexposed on the public internet [5][6]. Any workload sharing a physical network with cluster nodes gains access to the kubelet and control plane components, and VPC-based networking builds that segmentation by default instead of leaving it to manual firewall rules layered on top of a shared VLAN.

2. Network services and Load balancing scale natively

Under the vSphere Distributed Switch stack, every VIP in the environment runs through a single Foundation Load Balancer appliance pair in active/standby mode [4]. That’s a single point of scale for the whole Supervisor. VCF Networking with VPC distributes that load differently. A Virtual Network Appliance cluster can scale to up to ten nodes, running active/active, splitting VIPs, NAT, and other network services across the cluster instead of funneling them through one pair. A single network appliance can also host services for multiple VPCs, so the model scales both up, with more nodes, and out, with more tenants per node.

Organizations that need more load-balancing depth, or autoscaling tied to application metrics, can add VMware Avi Load Balancer. It integrates natively with both Supervisor networking stacks, and adds to the VPC benefits.

3. VPC networking, Connectivity, and Traceflow – all in vCenter

Every VPC workflow lives inside the vCenter networking tab, including diagnostics. Administrators view VPCs and their networks, configure the Virtual Network Appliance, and define Connectivity Policies that decide which VPCs can talk to each other and which stay isolated, all without leaving the tool they already use to run the rest of the environment [1]. Traceflow, also built into vCenter, lets an administrator trace a packet’s actual path between two VPC-connected workloads, or between a workload and an external IP address [1].

For a Network Decision Maker, that consolidation matters as much as any single feature. A separate networking console for Kubernetes traffic means a separate tool to license, a separate skill set to staff for, and a separate audit surface to secure. VPC networking folds Kubernetes connectivity, VM connectivity, policy, and diagnostics into one plane that the existing vSphere team already runs.

4. Easy onboarding and connectivity

VPC networking can be instantiated with just one VLAN, without requiring advanced network configurations in the network fabric[7]. Workload domain deployment in VCF is VPC-ready by default. The vmkernel interfaces needed for virtual networking are already configured, and the Virtual Network Appliance is already in place, so administrators typically only need to supply the VLAN and the external IP addresses. No Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) configuration and no NSX Edge cluster are required to get started.

From there, the architecture can grow without a redesign. Teams that need to avoid stretching a single VLAN across every host can move to a Centralized connection through an Edge cluster with static routing or BGP, or integrate directly with Cisco and Arista Ethernet Virtual Private Network (EVPN) and Virtual Extensible LAN (VXLAN) fabrics for distributed connectivity [10][11]. VCF 9.1 formalized this path, adding native EVPN interoperability with Arista Networks and expanded Cisco integration built for exactly this kind of growth.

5. VPCs unlock private cloud and ecosystem capabilities VLANs cannot

The gap between the two stacks widens once an organization wants to run Kubernetes and VMs as a self-service private cloud rather than a set of manually provisioned environments. VPC networking supports a full private cloud experience through VCF Automation, including multi-tenancy, blueprints, and self-service networking. The vSphere Distributed Switch path has no namespace create-read-update-delete capability from VCF Automation.

That private cloud foundation carries three adjacent capabilities with it. Broadcom is working directly with Cisco and Arista to deliver EVPN/VXLAN fabric integration, so VPC networks connect through one optimized fabric instead of a collection of manually managed VLANs [11]. VPC networking also integrates natively with Infoblox for DNS, DHCP, and IP address management, automating IP block allocation and DNS registration instead of requiring manual tracking]. And vDefend firewalling is fully VPC-aware, letting a security administrator define policy per VPC or between VPCs, with integration into the Antrea container network interface (CNI) and consumption directly from VCF Automation. A Supervisor running on the vSphere Distributed Switch stack can’t reach any of these, because that stack lacks the per-tenant, software-defined construct VPC provides.

Comparison of networking approaches

One nuance worth noting for planning purposes: as of VCF 9.1.1, administrators can also build a purely VLAN-backed VPC. It keeps the same operational model and vCenter workflow as a full-stack VPC, but consumes classless inter-domain routing (CIDR) blocks directly from the physical fabric instead of from an internal address space, which removes the ability to create private networks [1]. That option exists for environments that need the VPC operational model without an overlay network. It’s a configuration choice, not a limitation of VPC as an architecture.

The case for VPC networking

For decision makers evaluating or planning VCF 9.1 environments, the technical case for VPCs holds up across key attributes at scale: security exposure, load-balancing headroom, operational simplicity, and ecosystem integration. The practical case is just as strong for VCF and Kubernetes administrators handling the hands-on configuration. The VPC path starts as simply as a single VLAN and grows into Centralized connections, EVPN fabric integration, and full private cloud automation, all without requiring a redesign along the way [8][9[10].

The vSphere Distributed Switch stack still has a place. It suits VMware vSphere Foundation deployments and smaller or lab environments. But for any organization planning to run vSphere Kubernetes Service workloads at production scale, inside a private cloud model, VPC-based networking is the stack built for that destination, and VCF 9.1 marks it as recommended for exactly that reason.

Next Steps

Teams planning a Supervisor deployment can find the full technical reference, including packet walks, deployment procedures, and troubleshooting guides, in the VCF Networking Encyclopedia, maintained by Dimitri Desmidt [7]. For hands-on configuration guidance, VMware’s documentation on configuring Supervisor with VPC and the Distributed Transit Gateway walks through the vCenter workflow step by step.

  2. “Deploying Supervisor with VCF Networking with VPC.” Broadcom TechDocs, VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1, July 27, 2026.
  3. “Distributed VLAN Connectivity Model.” Broadcom TechDocs, VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1 Design Library, June 30, 2026.
  4. “vSphere Supervisor.” Broadcom TechDocs, vDefend Design Library, July 2, 2026.
  5. “Security Checklist.” The Kubernetes Project.
  6. “A Closer Look at NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance.” The Kubernetes Project, October 5, 2021.

item.content:encoded:
Holodeck 9.1.1, a patch release for the nested VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) toolkit, is now available. This release follows Holodeck 9.1 and focuses on deployment reliability, tighter prechecks, and added support for new versions.

Holodeck 9.1 introduced Virtual Network Appliance (VNA) cluster support and expanded VCF 9.1 coverage. It also introduced a long list of Day 2 operations improvements. Holodeck 9.1.1 builds on that foundation. Holodeck 9.1.1 adds support for VMware vSphere Foundation (VVF) and VCF 9.1.1. It also fixes bugs from the 9.1 release, and tightens the prechecks that catches deployment problems during prechecks.

A quick refresher

Holodeck is a self-contained, automated, and repeatable way to deploy nested VCF environments. It virtualizes the full management and workload domain stack, ships with built-in infrastructure services such as NTP, DNS, BGP, and DHCP, and runs on a single ESX host or a modest vSphere cluster. Teams use it to validate new VCF capabilities, train administrators, and reproduce support scenarios without reserving production hardware.

What’s new in Holodeck 9.1.1

Features

Holodeck 9.1.1 adds support for deploying VMware vSphere Foundation and VCF 9.1.1, and it supports greenfield deployment of VCF 9.1 patch releases more broadly, so you’re not stuck waiting for a new Holodeck release to test the latest patch. This release also adds support for custom VM and template folder structures when deploying to a vCenter target, giving administrators more control over how nested environments land in their existing inventory, allowing use of RBAC in vCenter.

Enhancements

Several changes in this release reduce failed deployments. Holodeck now checks online depot connectivity for 9.x environments before a deployment gets underway, and ovftool checks along with ISO and OVA guardrails catch issues earlier in the VCF Installer flow. Holodeck now relaxes precheck validation for 9.0.x ESX and VCF Installer binaries. This lets you deploy patch releases as greenfield deployments.

Dual-site BGP setups get their own bgpRouterConfiguration.yaml, alongside updated handling for GitLab, rc.local, and centralized transit gateway IP blocks. The HoloRouter OVA deployment flow now logs more detail when GitOps is enabled, and the Authentik configuration and network manager service handling inside the HoloRouter and Webtop flow have both been updated for reliability.

Bug fixes

This patch resolves multiple issues surfaced during 9.1 deployments. For the full list, see the release notes.

Supported versions

Holodeck 9.1.1 supports:

  • VCF 9.1.1.0, 9.1.0.0, 9.0.2.0, 9.0.1.0, and 9.0.0.0 (including patch releases for VCF 9.1)
  • VCF 5.2.4, 5.2.3, 5.2.2, 5.2.1, and 5.2

The minimum ESX version required on the physical server to deploy Holodeck is 8.0 U3.

Get started

If you’re already running Holodeck 9.1, upgrading to 9.1.1 gets you a more stable deployment experience with the same feature set you know. If you haven’t tried Holodeck yet, this patch is a good time to start: VMware vSphere Foundation and VCF 9.1.1 support means you can validate the latest patch release in a nested environment before it touches your production hardware.

For the complete list of features, enhancements, and bug fixes, read the Holodeck 9.1.1 release notes.

Ready to get started? Here are all the resources you need:

  • Download Holodeck 9.1.1 — Get the latest release and start deploying nested VCF environments today.
  • Report an Issue — Found a bug or have a feature request? Open an issue on GitHub and help us make Holodeck even better.

item.content:encoded:
A VCF Operations alert that detects new Services Runtime node VMs by name and IP address.

VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) management services in VCF 9.1.x run on VCF services runtime, a Kubernetes-based layer whose worker nodes are ordinary virtual machines in your management domain. When you scale out, perform upgrade operations, or when a node fails and is recovered, VCF services runtime deploys new worker node virtual machines for you. That is convenient, but it leaves operations teams with a question that sounds simple:

How do you know a new node was deployed, and which VM is it?

Until you can answer that reliably, everything downstream is manual. Nobody updates the Configuration Management Database (CMDB), nobody adds the virtual machine to the right vSphere DRS group, and nobody tells the monitoring team there is something new to watch. In this post we show how to build a precise, event-driven alert for worker node creation based on only the data collected by VCF Operations. Then we look at a number of different use cases, where we can perform various actions based on the alert being triggered.

What the alert gives you

When a new control plane or worker node virtual machine appears, VCF Operations will raise an alert against that virtual machine. The alert consists of the following details:

  • The VM name, exactly as it appears in vCenter
  • The guest IP address, reported by VMware Tools
  • A timestamp, and an alert object you can attach any notification to

Once the alert is triggered, any response or action depends on your organization’s specific needs. The rest of this post explains how the alert works, then covers use cases.

The vCenter adapter tracks each VM’s creation time, guest IP address, and uptime. The VCF management services adapter creates a vmsp-platform-node object for every real Kubernetes node and links it to its VM. So VCF Operations alerts on properties and relationships.

How the alert works

The alert is defined on the VM object type. It combines symptoms from the VM with a symptom from a related object, and all of them must be true at once.

On the VM:

On a related object (at least one child):

Identity comes from a relationship, not a name

A fair question is whether an ordinary VM, deployed by a user at the same moment, could be mistaken for a node. The first three conditions would not stop it. The fourth does.

The adapter links a node object to its VM using the node’s UUID, not its name or IP address. On a live node, the nodeUUID on the vmsp-platform-node object is identical to the summary|smbiosUUID on the vCenter VM object. A VM that was not provisioned as a cluster node would have a different hardware UUID and no vmsp-platform-node child, so the alert stays inactive for it, whatever it is called. A plain clone of a node VM gets a new SMBIOS UUID by default, so it does not match either.

Use case 1: Notify the team by email

The simplest response is a notification rule on the alert that sends email through your existing SMTP outbound plugin. Because of the “has an IP” symptom, the alert text contains both the VM name and its address, so the message is useful on its own: “a new node, sfo-sr01-abcde, is live at 10.11.x.x.”

Send it to the platform team, the monitoring team, or a shared mailbox that feeds a ticket queue. It is also the fallback: whatever else you automate, the email still tells a human what happened.

Two coarser alerts on the VCF services runtime cluster object, based on the new_resources and not_existing_resource_count counters, can complement it. They count every object under the cluster, including pods and volumes, so they fire on upgrades and do not name a node. Treat them as “something changed, take a look.”

Use case 2: Place the VM in a DRS VM group

In many environments VCF services runtime nodes are spread across availability zones with VM-Host rules. A new VM that is not in the right vSphere DRS VM group is a VM vSphere DRS may be placed anywhere, and someone has to remember to add it.

A second notification rule on the same alert can call a webhook that starts a VCF Operations orchestrator workflow. Ours does the following:

  1. Ignores cancel notifications. Operations also notifies when an alert clears.
  2. Finds the cluster and fails loudly if there is not exactly one match.
  3. Finds the VM by name as vCenter reports it, ignoring the request if it is not found and refusing to act if more than one VM has that name.
  4. Checks the VM runs on a host in the target cluster. This is the scope guard.
  5. Checks if the DRS VM group exists and whether the VM is already a member. If it is, nothing happens.
  6. Runs the built-in “Add virtual machines to DRS group” workflow and waits for it to finish.

Step 5 makes the workflow idempotent. Notifications repeat, and a node that reboots can raise the alert again, but the second run finds the VM already in the group and changes nothing. The workflow also supports a dry run: if the alert ID starts with dryrun, it runs every check and reports what it would do. Use it to test against a real VM without touching the group.

Because the workflow takes the VM name exactly as vCenter reports it and applies no naming filter, it works for any Services Runtime cluster, not just one. and applies no naming filter, it works for any Services Runtime cluster, not just one.

Use case 3: Keep your CMDB current

New infrastructure that never reaches the CMDB is a familiar audit finding. The alert already contains what a CMDB’s Configuration Item (CI) record needs: the VM name and the IP address. The same webhook pattern that adds a VM to a vSphere DRS group can create or update a configuration item instead, or as well:

  • Call your ITSM tool directly. An orchestrator workflow can call the REST API of ServiceNow or a similar platform to create a CI with the name, IP, platform and discovery time, using the alert as the trigger.
  • Open a ticket first. For environments where CI creation needs approval, create a change or task record from the alert and let the CMDB process take over.
  • Reconcile rather than create. Look up the CI by name, update it if it exists and create it if not, so repeated notifications do no harm.

The idempotent design from the vSphere DRS workflow carries over. The alert identifies a node, the workflow checks whether the record already exists, and it acts only when something is missing.

More use cases

  • Tag the VM in vCenter (for example with its platform and owner) so reporting policies pick it up.
  • Post to chat. Send the name and IP to the platform team’s channel through a webhook.
  • Confirm capacity. Compare the new node count against what you planned, and flag scale-outs nobody expected.
  • Start a compliance check. Trigger a baseline scan or a security review on each new node.

You wire these up exactly as the DRS rule is: a notification rule on the alert, pointing at an outbound plugin.

Wiring the webhook

A webhook outbound plugin in VCF Operations posts a JSON payload to the workflow’s REST endpoint. The payload carries values from the alert:

<code>{"parameters":[
 {"name":"alertName",    "type":"string","value":{"string":{"value":"${ALERT_DEFINITION}"}}},
 {"name":"resourceName", "type":"string","value":{"string":{"value":"${RESOURCE_NAME}"}}},
 {"name":"alertId",      "type":"string","value":{"string":{"value":"${ALERT_ID}"}}},
 {"name":"alertStatus",  "type":"string","value":{"string":{"value":"${ALERT_STATUS}"}}}
]}</code>

What to take away

  • Alert on what the platform already knows. When logs cannot be tied to an object, properties, metrics, and relationships usually can.
  • Use a relationship, not a name, to prove identity. Linking the VM to its node object through the hardware UUID is what stops a look-alike VM from triggering anything.
  • Treat the alert as a platform event. One reliable signal, with a name and an IP, can feed email, DRS placement, your CMDB, and more. Build the signal once, and add responses as you need them.
  • Make every action idempotent, and give it a dry run. Notification systems repeat themselves. An action that is safe to run twice, and can be tested without consequences, removes most of the fear from automation.

If you already run VCF Operations 9.1.x with the VCF management services adapter, you can build the alert in an afternoon: three symptoms on the VM, one on its child node object, and an email rule. Add a webhook and a workflow when you are ready to act on it. The harder, and more valuable, work is deciding what should happen automatically when platform changes occur.

item.content:encoded:
In 9.1, the VCF Download Tool (VCFDT) needs an activation code tied to an entitled site. A username and password don’t work in 9.x. If you’re a Broadcom partner or an employee, your portal login can usually download individual files from the Broadcom Support Portal, but it often can’t generate an activation code. That leaves you with a freshly deployed VCF Installer and nothing to install from.

You can still fill it. Download every file and the metadata by hand, build the depot folder structure yourself, copy it to the installer, and let VCFDT upload it. This post walks through that run from start to finish, and explains the one rule that trips most people up: the installer only accepts a component when every file the product version catalog lists for that bundle is present, in the right folder, at the right size. A bundle with even one missing file is skipped without a word.

Two Ways to Get Binaries In

If you’re a customer with entitlement, don’t do any of this. Follow the official VCFDT procedure in the Broadcom documentation. With a token or activation code, VCFDT pulls all files and the metadata for you, and every trap below goes away. If the installer has internet or proxy access, the online depot is simpler still.

If you’re a partner or building a lab without a token, you download everything by hand, build the depot layout, copy it over, and then follow steps 5 to 7 of the same article. The rest of this post is about that second path, because the article assumes VCFDT did the downloading and so says little about what the folders must look like.

The Lab

  • VCF Installer appliance: 9.1.1.0200.25801073, FQDN vcf-installer.vcf9.ai
  • VCFDT: vcf-download-tool-9.1.1.0200.25801073, a tar.gz extracted on the appliance
  • Workstation: Windows with WSL, where the Windows drive appears at /mnt/host/c/...
  • SSH to the installer as vcf. Root SSH is disabled by default, so use su - for the root steps
  • Depot root on the appliance: /nfs/vmware/vcf/nfs-mount/depot, which will contain PROD

The binaries total roughly 65 GB. Check the space before you start:

df -h /nfs/vmware/vcf/nfs-mount

Where the Files Come From

Everything is on the Broadcom Support Portal under the VCF 9.1.1 release, on each component’s download page. That includes the metadata and every yaml and plugin file. Component pages you’ll visit include Fleet Lifecycle, SDDC Lifecycle, Software Depot, Telemetry and VCF services runtime.

The yaml and plugin files are tiny, under 35 KB and some under 1 KB, so they’re easy to miss in a file list. Download them anyway. You’ll see why in a moment.

Take the patch builds that match your installer, which here means the .0100 and .0200 builds, not the 9.1.1.0 GA builds. The catalog only links files from the same build.

You don’t need any of these for a fleet install:

  • the ESX installer ISO (hosts are installed separately)
  • vSphere Supervisor
  • HCX
  • Native Storage Service
  • the optional VCF service entries
  • vsan-service-vmsp-backend

The Depot Layout

This is everything that ends up under /nfs/vmware/vcf/nfs-mount/depot/. Folder names are case-sensitive and come from the component names in productVersionCatalog.json. Don’t extract or rename any file.

Metadata first. It comes from the portal’s metadata download and must match the build level of the binaries:

PROD/metadata/manifest/v1/vcfManifest.json
PROD/metadata/productVersionCatalog/v1/productVersionCatalog.json
PROD/metadata/productVersionCatalog/v1/productVersionCatalog.sig
PROD/metadata/Compatibility/v1/VmwareCompatibilityData.json
PROD/metadata/Compatibility/v2/VmwareCompatibilityData.json
PROD/metadata/vsan/hcl/all.json
PROD/metadata/vsan/hcl/lastupdatedtime.json
PROD/vsan/hcl/all.json                                   (VCFDT reads this path)
PROD/vsan/hcl/lastupdatedtime.json
PROD/COMP/SDDC_MANAGER_VCF/Compatibility/VmwareCompatibilityData.json
PROD/COMP/VCENTER/vmw/8d167796-34d5-4899-be0a-6daade4005a3/upgrade_info.xml
PROD/COMP/VCENTER/vmw/8d167796-34d5-4899-be0a-6daade4005a3/upgrade_info.sig
PROD/COMP/VCENTER/vmw/8d167796-34d5-4899-be0a-6daade4005a3/upgrade_info.xml.sha256

Appliances need one file each, in PROD/COMP/<FOLDER>/:

SDDC_MANAGER_VCF/     VCF-SDDC-Manager-Appliance-9.1.1.0200.25801071.ova     (2.40 GB)
VCENTER/              VMware-VCSA-all-9.1.1.0100.25784172.iso                (9.69 GB)

Service packages need four files each: the package, a plugin, a configuration-schema yaml and a depot-manifest yaml. Same location, PROD/COMP/<FOLDER>/:

VCF_FLEET_LCM/   (Fleet lifecycle)
  vcf-fleet-lcm-9.1.1.0200.25801070.tgz

  depot-manifest-salt-raas-9.1.1.0100.25795075.yaml
TELEMETRY_ACCEPTOR/   (Telemetry)
  telemetry-acceptor-9.1.1.0100.25741214.tgz
  telemetry-acceptor-plugin-9.1.1.0100.25741214.tgz

  depot-manifest-telemetry-acceptor-9.1.1.0100.25741214.yaml
VIDB/   (Identity broker; note the plugin name)
  vidb-9.1.1.0100.25796677.tgz

  vcd-migrator-9.1.1.0200.25801570.tgz

  configuration-schema-vcd-migrator-9.1.1.0200.25801570.yaml
  depot-manifest-vcd-migrator-9.1.1.0200.25801570.yaml
VRA/   (VCF Automation, 15.69 GB; note the plugin name)
  vcfa-bundle-9.1.1.0200.25801570.tar
  vcfa-plugin-9.1.1.0200.25801570.tgz
  configuration-schema-vcfa-bundle-9.1.1.0200.25801570.yaml
  depot-manifest-vcfa-bundle-9.1.1.0200.25801570.yaml

The VCF services runtime needs six files, in PROD/COMP/VSP/ (16.11 GB):

vmsp-platform-9.1.1.0100.25801571.tar
vmsp-plugin-9.1.1.0100.25801571.tgz
vmsp-cli-9.1.1.0100.25801571.tar.gz
vcf-services-platform-template-9.1.1.0100.25801571.ova
configuration-schema-vmsp-platform-9.1.1.0100.25801571.yaml
depot-manifest-vmsp-platform-9.1.1.0100.25801571.yaml

The portal’s display names don’t match the folder names. Use this mapping:

Portal display name Folder
Fleet Lifecycle VCF_FLEET_LCM
SDDC Lifecycle VCF_SDDC_LCM
Software Depot DEPOT_SERVICE
Salt master VCF_SALT
Salt RaaS VCF_SALT_RAAS
Telemetry TELEMETRY_ACCEPTOR
Identity broker VIDB
VCF service – Migration service engine VCF_SERVICE_VCD_MIGRATION_BACKEND
VCF Automation VRA
VCF services runtime VSP

The Procedure

1. Deploy the VCF Installer Appliance

Nothing special here. Deploy it the usual way and make sure you can SSH to it as vcf.

2. Prepare the Folders

On the installer, as root:

mkdir -p /nfs/vmware/vcf/nfs-mount/depot /nfs/vmware/vcf/nfs-mount/vcfdt
chown vcf:vcf /nfs/vmware/vcf/nfs-mount/depot /nfs/vmware/vcf/nfs-mount/vcfdt

3. Copy the Downloads to the Installer

Download every file listed above from the portal into one folder on the workstation. Then copy it from WSL. Install rsync first if you don’t have it:

sudo apt install -y rsync
rsync -rtvP /mnt/host/c/Users/<user>/Downloads/<folder>/ vcf@<installer-fqdn>:/nfs/vmware/vcf/nfs-mount/depot/

Use -rtvP rather than -aP. Files on a Windows mount carry odd permissions, and -a would try to preserve them. Mind the trailing slashes, which decide whether you copy the folder’s contents or the folder itself. -P lets an interrupted copy resume, which you’ll appreciate with a 16 GB file.

4. Sort the Flat Files into the Component Folders

Important

The folder structure and file names are what VCFDT reads to find the binaries. It looks in PROD/COMP/<FOLDER> for the file names the product version catalog lists, and the folder names must match the catalog’s component names, case included. A file in the wrong folder, a renamed or extracted file, or a missing yaml or plugin file means the bundle is skipped without an error, and that component never reaches the VCF Installer. Keep every file as downloaded and let the loop below place it.

The files landed flat in the depot root. As root, from the depot root, this loop moves each one into PROD/COMP/<FOLDER>:

cd /nfs/vmware/vcf/nfs-mount/depot
for f in *; do
  [ -f "$f" ] || continue
  b=${f#configuration-schema-}; b=${b#depot-manifest-}
  case "$b" in
    VCF-SDDC-Manager-Appliance-*) d=SDDC_MANAGER_VCF ;;
    VMware-VCSA-all-*)            d=VCENTER ;;
    nsx-unified-appliance-*)      d=NSX_T_MANAGER ;;
    Operations-Appliance-*)       d=VROPS ;;
    Operations-Cloud-Proxy-*)     d=VCF_OPS_CLOUD_PROXY ;;
    Vcf-License-Server-*)         d=VCF_LICENSE_SERVER ;;
    vcfa-*)                       d=VRA ;;
    vidb-*)                       d=VIDB ;;
    vcf-fleet-lcm-*)              d=VCF_FLEET_LCM ;;
    vcf-sddc-lcm-*)               d=VCF_SDDC_LCM ;;
    vcf-fleet-depot-*)            d=DEPOT_SERVICE ;;
    salt-raas-*)                  d=VCF_SALT_RAAS ;;
    salt-*)                       d=VCF_SALT ;;
    telemetry-acceptor-*)         d=TELEMETRY_ACCEPTOR ;;
    vcd-migrator-*)               d=VCF_SERVICE_VCD_MIGRATION_BACKEND ;;
    vmsp-*|vcf-services-platform-*) d=VSP ;;
    *) echo "SKIP $f"; continue ;;
  esac
  mkdir -p PROD/COMP/$d && mv -v "$f" PROD/COMP/$d/
done

A few things in that loop are deliberate:

  • salt-raas-* has to be matched before salt-*, or the Salt RaaS files end up in the Salt master folder.
  • Match vcfa-*, not vcfa-bundle-*, so that vcfa-plugin lands in VRA along with the bundle.
  • vcf-services-platform-template goes to VSP, which is why the last pattern has two alternatives.
  • The prefix strip at the top sends each yaml to the same folder as its package.

To use it, run it as root from the depot root, as shown. It only looks at regular files sitting directly in that folder, so PROD and anything already sorted is left alone, and it’s safe to run again after you copy in more files. Anything it doesn’t recognise prints SKIP <name> and stays where it is, which tells you to check the file name or add a pattern.

Sorting by hand means placing 48 files into 16 folders, and the plugin and yaml files are the ones that end up in the wrong folder or get forgotten. The loop sorts them the same way every time, so the ordering rules above are written down once instead of remembered for every file.

5. Copy the Metadata into PROD

Put the metadata files at the paths shown in the layout above, exactly. VCFDT reads fixed locations, and a file one folder off is the same as a file that isn’t there.

6. Extract VCFDT

Extract the VCFDT tar.gz under /nfs/vmware/vcf/nfs-mount/vcfdt. The bin folder you’ll run it from in step 9 sits under that path.

7. Fix Ownership and Permissions

As root:

chown -R vcf_lcm:vcf /nfs/vmware/vcf/nfs-mount/depot
find /nfs/vmware/vcf/nfs-mount/depot -type d -exec chmod 755 {} ;
find /nfs/vmware/vcf/nfs-mount/depot -type f -exec chmod 644 {} ;

This step looks cosmetic and isn’t. The troubleshooting section explains why the upload fails without it. Run it again any time you copy something new into the depot as vcf.

8. Verify Every Bundle against the Catalog

Before you upload anything, check the depot against the product version catalog. The script below reads productVersionCatalog.json, finds each INSTALL bundle that matches a file in each folder, and checks that every file the bundle lists exists at the catalog’s exact size.

import json, os
P = '/nfs/vmware/vcf/nfs-mount/depot/PROD/metadata/productVersionCatalog/v1/productVersionCatalog.json'
C = '/nfs/vmware/vcf/nfs-mount/depot/PROD/COMP'
bundles = []
def walk(o):
    if isinstance(o, dict):
        if 'binaries' in o and 'id' in o: bundles.append(o)
        for v in o.values(): walk(v)
    elif isinstance(o, list):
        for v in o: walk(v)
walk(json.load(open(P)))
for comp in sorted(os.listdir(C)):
    d = os.path.join(C, comp)
    if not os.path.isdir(d): continue
    have = set(os.listdir(d))
    for b in bundles:
        if b.get('type') != 'INSTALL': continue
        if not have.intersection(x['fileName'] for x in b['binaries']): continue
        print(f"== {comp}  bundle {b['id']}")
        for x in b['binaries']:
            f = os.path.join(d, x['fileName'])
            st = 'MISSING' if not os.path.exists(f) else ('OK' if os.path.getsize(f) == x.get('size') else 'WRONG SIZE')
            print(f"   {st:<12} {x['fileName']}")

Save it with vi rather than pasting a heredoc into the terminal, which can mangle the indentation. Every line must say OK before you upload.

A check based on file name patterns isn’t enough here. Plugin names don’t follow one pattern (vidb-upgrade-plugin, vcfa-plugin), so a pattern-based check passes folders that are missing a file. Reading the catalog is the only way to know what each bundle really wants.

To use it, save it as check-depot.py with vi and run python3 check-depot.py as root. It changes nothing and only prints. The two paths at the top, P for the catalog and C for PROD/COMP, match the depot root used in this post, so edit them if yours is somewhere else. Each folder gets a heading with the catalog’s bundle ID, then one line per required file marked OK, MISSING or WRONG SIZE. Pipe it through tee if you want a copy of the output to work from.

The installer skips an incomplete bundle without telling you, so the first sign of a missing file is a component that never shows up, usually after a long upload. The script turns that into a list of exactly which file is missing or the wrong size, before you upload anything. Doing the same check by hand means opening the pretty-printed catalog and comparing the listed size of every file with what’s on disk, for 48 files. The script does it in a few seconds and reads the file list from the catalog itself, so it catches the oddly named plugin files that a name-based check misses.

9. Upload

cd /nfs/vmware/vcf/nfs-mount/vcfdt/bin
./vcf-download-tool binaries upload --depot-store /nfs/vmware/vcf/nfs-mount/depot --sddc-manager-fqdn vcf-installer.vcf9.ai --sddc-manager-user admin@local --sddc-manager-user-password-file <password file>

--depot-store points at the folder that contains PROD, not at PROD itself. On the first run VCFDT asks whether to trust the installer’s certificate. Answer yes. Keep the SSH session open, because the two 16 GB components take a while. Delete the password file when you’re done.

10. Check Binary Management

In the installer UI, open Binary Management for VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.1.0. Online Depot and Offline Depot both show as not configured. That’s expected when you side-load.

How the Upload Decides What to Accept

Knowing what VCFDT does makes the failures easier to read.

It starts with metadata, uploading in a fixed order: vSAN HCL, compatibility data, the unified release manifest, the product version catalog, and the vCenter upgrade info. It only indexes binaries after all five succeed.

Then it scans each component folder against the catalog’s bundles. Each bundle entry lists every file name with a checksum, a size and a tag: BINARY, BINARY_SCHEMA, DEPOT_MANIFEST or PLUGIN_BINARY. If every listed file is there, VCFDT logs “local files exist (OCI verification disabled)” and queues the bundle. If one is missing, it logs “has missing local files” and skips the bundle. Nothing on the console tells you that happened. The only hint is a smaller element count.

Appliances have a single INSTALL bundle each. Service packages show up twice, as an INSTALL bundle and a PATCH bundle that share the same files. Six appliances plus ten service components gives 26 bundles.

Once a bundle is queued, the console prints “Uploading binary for Component: …” and polls IN_PROGRESS every 10 seconds until it reaches SUCCESSFUL. A Binary Upload Summary table closes the run.

After a successful upload, VCFDT deletes the uploaded binaries from the depot (“Cleaning binary files … after successful upload”). Re-running is safe. Components already at Success stay at Success, and the manifest step logs LCM_MANIFEST_ALREADY_EXISTS and still reports success.

Troubleshooting

“The SSO credentials for user vcf are not correct or the SSO account is locked.”

You passed the OS user to the tool. Use the installer’s local admin instead: --sddc-manager-user admin@local.

Metadata Files Not Found

You’ll see a NoSuchFileException for PROD/vsan/hcl/all.json, VmwareCompatibilityData.json or vcfManifest.json. Put the metadata at the exact paths in the layout above. Note that all.json is needed in two places: under PROD/metadata/vsan/hcl/ and under PROD/vsan/hcl/.

INSUFFICIENT_PRODUCT_VERSION_CATALOG_READ_PERMISSIONS or INSUFFICIENT_VCENTER_UPGRADE_INFO_READ_PERMISSIONS

This one is confusing because the log can say “Signature in productVersionCatalog.sig is valid” right before it fails.

VCFDT runs as vcf and streams some files itself. For the catalog and the vCenter upgrade info, though, it only passes the path, and the installer’s LCM service reads the file from disk as vcf_lcm. Folders created by the vcf account are private (drwx------), so vcf_lcm can’t get in. Running namei -l on the file path shows which folder is blocking it.

The fix is step 7. To verify it, read the file as vcf_lcm:

su -s /bin/bash vcf_lcm -c "cat <file> > /dev/null && echo OK"

Re-run step 7 after you copy anything new in as vcf.

File Does Not Exist at the Password File Path

The path to installer-password.txt is wrong for the user running the tool. Check it from the same account.

Only the Appliances Upload and the Service Packages Stay “Not downloaded”

Someone downloaded only the .tgz or .tar package without its yaml and plugin files. Download all four files per package (six for VSP) and run the step 8 script.

The Upload Lists “0 elements” and Nothing Uploads

The files look right and nothing happens. The cause is a missing plugin file or the VSP template OVA, which name-based checks don’t catch. Read the catalog entry to see every file the bundle requires:

grep -n -B30 -A20 '"fileName": "<file>"' PROD/metadata/productVersionCatalog/v1/productVersionCatalog.json

The catalog is pretty-printed JSON, so grep -o on a single line shows nothing useful.

“Failed to load the token … /etc/security/token/token.properties (Permission denied)”

This appears on every run as vcf. It’s harmless.

The Outcome

All 26 bundles uploaded with status SUCCESS and none failed. The six appliances have one INSTALL bundle. The ten service components have both INSTALL and PATCH:

Folder Component Version Bundles
VCF_LICENSE_SERVER License server 9.1.1.0100.25795080 INSTALL
SDDC_MANAGER_VCF SDDC Manager 9.1.1.0200.25801071 INSTALL
NSX_T_MANAGER VMware NSX 9.1.1.0100.25762940 INSTALL
VROPS VCF Operations 9.1.1.0100.25795063 INSTALL
VCENTER VMware vCenter 9.1.1.0100.25784172 INSTALL
VCF_OPS_CLOUD_PROXY Cloud proxy 9.1.1.0100.25795064 INSTALL
VSP VCF services runtime 9.1.1.0100.25801571 INSTALL + PATCH
VRA VCF Automation 9.1.1.0200.25801570 INSTALL + PATCH
VCF_SALT Salt master 9.1.1.0100.25795075 INSTALL + PATCH
VIDB Identity broker 9.1.1.0100.25796677 INSTALL + PATCH
VCF_SERVICE_VCD_MIGRATION_BACKEND Migration service engine 9.1.1.0200.25801570 INSTALL + PATCH
VCF_FLEET_LCM Fleet lifecycle 9.1.1.0200.25801070 INSTALL + PATCH
VCF_SDDC_LCM SDDC lifecycle 9.1.1.0200.25801981 INSTALL + PATCH
TELEMETRY_ACCEPTOR Telemetry 9.1.1.0100.25741214 INSTALL + PATCH
DEPOT_SERVICE Software depot 9.1.1.0200.25801072 INSTALL + PATCH
VCF_SALT_RAAS Salt RaaS 9.1.1.0100.25795075 INSTALL + PATCH

Binary Management for VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.1.0 now shows all 16 components at Success:

Component Version Size
Cloud proxy 9.1.1.0100 3.22 GB
Fleet lifecycle 9.1.1.0200 582.57 MB
Identity broker 9.1.1.0100 858.77 MB
License server 9.1.1.0100 884.16 MB
Migration service engine 9.1.1.0200 524.67 MB
Salt master 9.1.1.0100 393.84 MB

SDDC lifecycle 9.1.1.0200 650.06 MB
SDDC Manager 9.1.1.0200 2.40 GB
Software depot 9.1.1.0200 879.89 MB
Telemetry 9.1.1.0100 240.50 MB
VCF Automation 9.1.1.0200 15.69 GB
VCF Operations 9.1.1.0100 3.14 GB
VCF services runtime 9.1.1.0100 16.11 GB
VMware NSX 9.1.1.0100 8.26 GB
VMware vCenter 9.1.1.0100 9.69 GB

The Download Summary for 9.1.1.0 shows VMware vSphere Foundation and VMware Cloud Foundation both as “Downloaded”. The installer is ready for fleet deployment.

Two More Things

Note

This is a 9.1-specific step. After the fleet deploys, the management component binaries also have to be uploaded into the new Fleet Depot Service when you aren’t using an offline depot.

If you can get a customer token or activation code, use it. VCFDT then pulls all files and metadata itself, and none of the layout rules above apply. The online depot is easier again if the installer has internet or proxy access.

item.content:encoded:
Open source has always been foundational to cloud-native computing. Kubernetes itself is the product of thousands of contributors, but the platforms we build around it depend on an even broader ecosystem of projects spanning networking, storage, identity, backup and recovery, cluster lifecycle management, and more.

At Broadcom, contributing to that ecosystem has long meant more than consuming open source software. Our engineers contribute code, participate in communities, work alongside maintainers, and help projects evolve based on what we learn from running cloud-native technologies at enterprise scale.

Increasingly, we’re also thinking about another dimension of that responsibility: security.

The cloud-native world is expanding, and AI is shifting how we build and secure software. That opens up fresh ways to catch security risks while doubling down on what always works, which is direct, open collaboration with upstream communities.

Security Is a Shared Responsibility

Cloud-native infrastructure is inherently interconnected and a Kubernetes environment isn’t simply Kubernetes. It depends on projects responsible for cluster lifecycle, identity, storage, networking, backup and recovery, and many other capabilities. A security improvement in one of those projects can benefit far more than a single product or vendor.

That’s one reason we’ve expanded some of our upstream work to include proactive security research across open source projects that are important to the cloud-native ecosystem.

Our engineers work across projects including etcd, Cluster API, Pinniped, and Velero, where they work to identify potential issues, investigate them with project maintainers, and help move validated findings toward resolution.

The objective isn’t simply to find more vulnerabilities. It’s to help make the software that all of us depend on safer and more resilient.

Finding an Issue Is Only the Beginning

One thing this work has reinforced is that identifying a potential security issue and resolving one are very different things.

Modern AI tools can help engineers analyze large codebases and surface potential problems at a scale that would have been extraordinarily difficult through manual analysis alone. That’s a powerful capability, and one we believe can augment the work security researchers and software engineers are already doing.

But an AI-generated finding isn’t automatically a vulnerability.

Someone still has to understand the code. Is the behavior actually exploitable? Under what conditions? Which versions are affected? Is the proposed remediation appropriate? Could a fix introduce a regression somewhere else?

And in open source, there’s another critical participant in that process: the maintainer.

Maintainers understand the architecture, history, and operational realities of their projects. Responsible security work therefore requires collaboration by bringing potential findings to the appropriate project, validating them together, developing and reviewing fixes, and coordinating disclosure and releases when necessary.

AI can accelerate parts of that process. It doesn’t replace it.

From Findings to Upstream Fixes

We have seen the tangible impact of that upstream collaboration across several core projects: 

  • Velero: The work contributed directly to fixes for two published GitHub Security Advisories in the 1.18.3 release.
  • etcd: Research not only resolved issues across supported release branches but also updated the project’s threat model.
  • Cluster API and Pinniped: Findings were validated with community maintainers to deliver upstream remediations.

Project Highlights

  • Velero (v1.18.3): Coordinated and resolved security advisories GHSA-vrfp-2×59-hcfm and GHSA-8gv3-c356-fw76 upstream in release v1.18.3 (integrated downstream in VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) Add-ons v3.7.0+20260924), authoring patch remediation and performing end-to-end backup/restore validation.
  • etcd (v3.5.33 / v3.6.14 / v3.7.1): Discovered and disclosed CVE-2026-73500, contributed upstream patch remediation backported across releases v3.5.33, v3.6.14, and v3.7.1 (integrated downstream in vSphere Kubernetes Release (VKr) Oct Releases), and updated distributed state storage threat models.
  • Cluster API (v1.12.11, v1.13.5, v1.14.0): Screened and validated findings upstream, contributing bug fixes and hardening controller reconciliation logic.
  • Pinniped (v0.47.0): Identified authentication credential handling vulnerabilities under CVE-2026-59269, developed upstream remediation released in v0.47.0 (integrated downstream in VKr Oct Releases), and verified identity provider integration tests.

Impact by the Numbers

*Validated as Fixed Upstream: Pull Request with a fix was merged upstream and cherry picked when appropriate.

From AI Findings to Upstream Security Improvements

Identifying potential vulnerabilities is only the beginning. Turning AI-generated findings into meaningful security improvements requires careful validation, collaboration with upstream maintainers, and an understanding of each project’s architecture and threat model.

As Pushkar Joglekar, a Kubernetes maintainer who led this vulnerability discovery research, explained, an important part of the process was ensuring that findings were reviewed from a maintainer’s perspective before being shared with upstream projects.

“One non-negotiable requirement was to have every AI-generated finding filtered through a maintainer persona, so that when we request maintainer review time – a highly constrained resource – we are not wasting it by disclosing raw findings, which are often overstated or reflect intentional design decisions.”

This approach helped ensure that maintainer attention was focused on findings that warranted further investigation rather than potential issues already understood or accounted for in the project’s design.

For etcd, this collaboration also created opportunities to strengthen how security issues are evaluated. Benjamin Wang, an etcd maintainer, described how the work extended beyond validating vulnerabilities and developing patches to refining the project’s threat model and clarifying vulnerability boundaries.

These outcomes were not limited to identifying security vulnerabilities. In the Cluster API project, the research also provided opportunities to evaluate existing security practices and identify areas for additional hardening.

As longtime Cluster API maintainers Fabrizio Pandini and Stefan Büringer observed:

“Usage of AI models provides a new valuable source of input for this work, which led to a series of useful robustness / hardening improvements.”

They also emphasized that the absence of major findings reinforced the value of the project’s established security processes and ongoing collaboration with the Kubernetes Security Response Committee.

Together, these experiences demonstrate that AI-assisted vulnerability discovery is most valuable when paired with maintainer expertise and established upstream security practices. The result is not simply more findings, but better-informed security decisions and opportunities to strengthen the resilience of the projects the cloud-native ecosystem depends on.

Strengthening the Ecosystem We All Depend On

There is a tendency in technology to talk about open source contribution primarily in terms of features: a new capability contributed upstream, a new project donated to a foundation, or a new integration built with another project.

Those contributions matter.

But maintaining a healthy open source ecosystem also means doing some of the less visible work required to make that ecosystem dependable. This includes testing, reviewing, fixing, documenting, maintaining, and increasingly, proactively looking for ways to improve security.

For Broadcom, that’s an important part of what upstream participation means.

We build products using cloud-native open source technologies. Our customers rely on those technologies. Our engineers participate in the communities that maintain them.

When we combine our engineering expertise with emerging tools like AI to identify an issue, collaborate with maintainers, and contribute an improvement upstream, the benefit extends well beyond Broadcom.

It strengthens the shared foundation we’re all building on.

And as cloud-native infrastructure becomes the foundation for the next generation of applications and AI workloads, continuing to invest in that foundation may be one of the most important contributions we can make.
